seo.description: 45 fashion and clothing brand logos with names, explained by a brand designer: luxury houses like Gucci, Chanel, and Hermès, designer labels, accessories, and streetwear.

description: 45 fashion and clothing brand logos with names, explained by a brand designer: luxury houses like Gucci, Chanel, and Hermès, designer labels, accessories, and streetwear.
intro:
Fashion logos have to work on a shopping bag, a clothing label, a belt buckle, and a phone screen, and the best ones become so famous that people buy products just to wear them. Most of them are surprisingly simple: a founder's name in carefully chosen type, sometimes paired with a monogram or an emblem.

What makes a good fashion logo?

A name, set beautifully: most fashion brands are named after their founders, like Chanel, Dior, and Ralph Lauren, so the wordmark is the logo. The choice of typeface does all the work.

A monogram that becomes a pattern: the Gucci GG, the Louis Vuitton LV, and the Fendi FF are printed on bags and fabrics, so the monogram becomes the product itself.

Typography that signals the price point: high-contrast serifs feel like couture, wide sans serifs feel modern and minimal, and handwritten scripts feel personal.

Below are 45 fashion brand logos with names, in five groups: luxury fashion houses, Paris and Milan labels, designer brands, shoes, bags and accessories, and streetwear and high street. Each logo has a slide with my handwritten notes and a short explanation. If you are building a premium label, see how I approach luxury branding, and read my guides to monogram logos, wordmark logos, and logo fonts.

logoResearch.name: Gucci
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Guccio Gucci founded the house in Florence in 1921, and the interlocking GG monogram was introduced in the 1960s.
observations: Two mirrored G's lock together into a single round mark, built from the founder's initials.
A light, classic serif wordmark sits above the monogram, so the symbol does the heavy lifting.

logoResearch.name: Louis Vuitton
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Louis Vuitton opened his Paris trunk workshop in 1854, and his son Georges created the LV monogram canvas in 1896.
observations: The serif L and V overlap so tightly that they read as one letterform.
The full name is set tiny underneath, because the monogram is recognized on its own.

logoResearch.name: Chanel
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gabrielle "Coco" Chanel opened her first boutique in Paris in 1910, and the house still signs everything with this bold geometric wordmark.
observations: Wide, geometric capitals give the name a modern, architectural feel that has barely changed in a century.
Generous letter spacing and pure black make it look confident without any symbol.

logoResearch.name: Hermès
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Thierry Hermès founded the company as a harness workshop in Paris in 1837, and the Duc carriage logo has been used since the 1950s.
observations: The horse-drawn carriage tells the brand's origin story: it started by making harnesses and saddles.
Notably, the carriage has no driver, which is often read as the brand providing the craft and the customer taking the reins.

logoResearch.name: Prada
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Mario Prada and his brother opened their leather goods shop in Milan's Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II in 1913.
observations: The flared serif capitals and the R with its curled leg make the wordmark instantly recognizable.
The wide, heavy letters feel like an engraved shop sign, a nod to the brand's 1913 Milan store.

logoResearch.name: Dior
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Christian Dior founded his couture house in Paris in 1946 and launched the famous New Look the following year.
observations: High-contrast Didone letters, with very thin and very thick strokes, signal couture and elegance.
Dropping "Christian" leaves four tall letters that work as a monogram and a wordmark at once.

logoResearch.name: Fendi
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Adele and Edoardo Fendi founded the brand in Rome in 1925, and Karl Lagerfeld designed the FF "Zucca" monogram in 1965.
observations: The double F mark, one letter flipped, creates a compact pattern that also works as a print.
A heavy, condensed sans serif wordmark makes Fendi feel more modern than most Italian houses.

logoResearch.name: Versace
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Gianni Versace founded the house in Milan in 1978 and chose the Medusa head from Greek mythology as its emblem.
observations: Medusa represents fatal attraction: a mythological figure who made everyone who looked at her fall under her spell.
The widely spaced serif capitals keep the classical theme going below the emblem.

logoResearch.name: Burberry
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Thomas Burberry founded the company in 1856, and in 2023 the brand returned to a serif wordmark and its Equestrian Knight emblem.
observations: The 2023 serif wordmark replaced the plain sans serif from 2018, bringing back a sense of British heritage.
Narrow, tall capitals give the name a classic, tailored feel, like the trench coat it is famous for.

logoResearch.name: Givenchy
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hubert de Givenchy founded his house in Paris in 1952, and the 4G monogram dates from the brand's early years.
observations: Four square G's are arranged into a grid that reads like a modern, almost architectural emblem.
The spaced sans serif wordmark under the mark keeps the whole logo clean and graphic.

logoResearch.name: Balenciaga
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Cristóbal Balenciaga opened his first house in San Sebastián, Spain, in 1917 and moved to Paris in 1937.
observations: The 2017 wordmark is a wide sans serif with stretched letters, similar to the style used on bus stops and signage.
Removing all decoration makes the logo feel provocative and almost anti-luxury, which suits the brand.

logoResearch.name: Saint Laurent
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Yves Saint Laurent founded the house in Paris in 1961, and in 2012 creative director Hedi Slimane renamed the ready-to-wear line Saint Laurent.
observations: The bold Helvetica-style wordmark replaced "Yves Saint Laurent" for the ready-to-wear line.
The famous YSL monogram by Cassandre still exists for bags and beauty, so the wordmark can stay plain.

logoResearch.name: Celine
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Céline Vipiana founded the brand in Paris in 1945, and in 2018 Hedi Slimane removed the accent from the name.
observations: Dropping the accent on the É made the name look cleaner and more international.
Wide, round letters with even spacing give the wordmark a calm, confident look.

logoResearch.name: Valentino
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Valentino Garavani founded the house in Rome in 1960, and the V in an oval is the brand's signature emblem.
observations: The serif V inside an oval works like a seal or a monogram on hardware and packaging.
The brand uses the founder's first name, set in classic Roman serif capitals.

logoResearch.name: Giorgio Armani
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Giorgio Armani and Sergio Galeotti founded the company in Milan in 1975.
observations: Very condensed, thin capitals make the full name fit in one elegant line.
The understated type matches Armani's reputation for soft tailoring and quiet colors.

logoResearch.name: Dolce & Gabbana
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana founded the brand in Milan in 1985.
observations: The two founders' surnames sit side by side, joined by a tiny ampersand.
A bold, geometric sans serif keeps the long name readable on labels and storefronts.

logoResearch.name: Bottega Veneta
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Bottega Veneta was founded in Vicenza, Italy, in 1966, and is known for its woven intrecciato leather.
observations: The spaced serif capitals are quiet, which suits a brand famous for having no visible logo on its bags.
Its old slogan, "When your own initials are enough", explains why the logo stays so modest.

logoResearch.name: Loewe
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Loewe was founded in Madrid in 1846, which makes it one of the oldest luxury houses in the world.
observations: The 2014 wordmark, made under creative director Jonathan Anderson, uses a refined serif with flared strokes.
The round O stands out between straight letters, giving the short name its rhythm.

logoResearch.name: Ralph Lauren
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Ralph Lauren started the company in New York in 1967 by selling neckties under the name Polo.
observations: Widely spaced serif capitals give the founder's name a classic, Ivy League feel.
The famous Polo pony is a separate sub-brand mark, so the main wordmark stays purely typographic.

logoResearch.name: Calvin Klein
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Calvin Klein and Barry Schwartz founded the company in New York in 1968.
observations: A clean geometric sans serif makes the founder's name look modern and minimal.
Tight, even spacing lets the logo work as large as a billboard and as small as a waistband.

logoResearch.name: Tommy Hilfiger
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tommy Hilfiger launched his label in New York in 1985.
observations: The small flag in red, white, and navy has become the brand's most recognizable element.
Spaced capitals on both sides of the flag give the logo a preppy, American look.

logoResearch.name: Marc Jacobs
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Marc Jacobs founded his label in New York in 1984.
observations: Very wide letter spacing turns the founder's name into a clean, airy wordmark.
Geometric capitals with no decoration let the logo sit easily on bags, perfume, and labels.

logoResearch.name: Alexander McQueen
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Lee Alexander McQueen founded his label in London in 1992, and the brand now signs its logo simply as McQueen.
observations: The small c set inside the Q is a playful detail that makes the short name memorable.
Wide serif capitals balance the brand's dark, theatrical image with classic tailoring.

logoResearch.name: Stella McCartney
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Stella McCartney launched her label in 2001, and it has never used leather or fur.
observations: The letters are drawn with dots, giving the logo a light, almost stitched feel.
The very wide spacing and thin construction make the wordmark feel gentle and modern.

logoResearch.name: Vivienne Westwood
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Vivienne Westwood opened her first shop with Malcolm McLaren on London's King's Road in 1971.
observations: The bold, slanted serif script has the attitude of the brand's punk roots.
The two names stack on top of each other, so the logo works like a badge or a label.

logoResearch.name: Paul Smith
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Paul Smith opened his first shop in Nottingham, England, in 1970.
observations: The logo is based on Paul Smith's own handwriting, so it feels personal and friendly.
A signature-style logo suits a brand known for playful details and colourful stripes.

logoResearch.name: Hugo Boss
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Hugo Boss was founded in Metzingen, Germany, in 1924, and in 2021 the main line was rebranded simply as BOSS.
observations: The 2021 wordmark is heavy, wide, and all caps, designed to stand out on social media.
Shortening the name to four letters made the logo bolder and easier to read at small sizes.

logoResearch.name: Jimmy Choo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jimmy Choo was co-founded in London in 1996 by shoemaker Jimmy Choo and Tamara Mellon.
observations: Thin, wide capitals give the founder's name a light, elegant feel, like a stiletto heel.
The wordmark keeps the brand looking polished on shoe boxes and soles.

logoResearch.name: Christian Louboutin
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Christian Louboutin founded his shoe brand in Paris in 1991, and its red lacquered soles became a signature.
observations: The logo is a flowing signature, which makes the brand feel personal and handmade.
A small "Christian" sits above a large, swirling surname with a long flourish.

logoResearch.name: Coach
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Coach was founded in New York in 1941 as a family-run leather workshop.
observations: The frame around the name looks like a stamped leather tag, a nod to the brand's craft.
Heavy serif capitals make the short name feel solid and durable.

logoResearch.name: Michael Kors
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Michael Kors launched his label in New York in 1981.
observations: A clean, geometric sans serif makes the founder's name easy to read on bags and watches.
The even, generous spacing keeps the logo modern and approachable.

logoResearch.name: Kate Spade
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Kate and Andy Spade founded the brand in New York in 1993, starting with handbags.
observations: The spade symbol is a witty play on the founder's surname.
The lowercase serif wordmark and small "new york" line make the logo feel friendly and feminine.

logoResearch.name: Tory Burch
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Tory Burch launched her label in New York in 2004.
observations: The double T medallion between the names works as a monogram on hardware, shoes, and bags.
Wide capitals on each side make the logo symmetrical and balanced.

logoResearch.name: Longchamp
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Jean Cassegrain founded Longchamp in Paris in 1948, naming it after the Longchamp racecourse.
observations: Very wide letter spacing gives the name a light, elegant feel.
The small "Paris" line underneath connects the brand to its French origins.

logoResearch.name: Ferragamo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Salvatore Ferragamo founded the brand in Florence in 1927, and in 2022 the house dropped "Salvatore" with a new wordmark by Peter Saville.
observations: The 2022 logo replaced the founder's signature with clean, wide capitals.
Dropping the first name and the script made the brand feel younger and more modern.

logoResearch.name: Miu Miu
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Miuccia Prada founded Miu Miu in 1993, naming it after her childhood nickname.
observations: Rounded, chunky letters make the logo look playful and youthful.
Repeating the same word creates a pattern, like a label on a school uniform.

logoResearch.name: Off-White
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Virgil Abloh founded Off-White in Milan in 2013.
observations: A plain, bold sans serif looks like a label on industrial packaging, which fits the brand's ironic style.
The trademark symbol is part of the logo, turning a legal mark into a design detail.

logoResearch.name: Supreme
logoResearch.verifiedFact: James Jebbia opened the first Supreme store in New York in 1994.
observations: White Futura Heavy Oblique on a red box makes the logo instantly recognizable.
The box style was inspired by the work of artist Barbara Kruger.

logoResearch.name: Stüssy
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Shawn Stussy founded the brand in Laguna Beach, California, in 1980, starting with surfboards.
observations: The logo is his graffiti-style signature, the same one he wrote on his surfboards.
The rough, hand-drawn strokes gave streetwear its look long before it was mainstream.

logoResearch.name: Moncler
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Moncler was founded in 1952 in Monestier-de-Clermont, near Grenoble, and its name is an abbreviation of that town.
observations: The thin, wide capitals feel light and premium, like the brand's down jackets.
The name itself tells the brand's mountain origin story.

logoResearch.name: Acne Studios
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Acne Studios was founded in Stockholm in 1996, and Acne stands for "Ambition to Create Novel Expressions".
observations: The rounded sans serif looks friendly and slightly quirky, like the brand itself.
The full name, with "Studios", reflects the brand's start as a creative collective.

logoResearch.name: Zara
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Amancio Ortega opened the first Zara store in A Coruña, Spain, in 1975, and the current logo was introduced in 2019.
observations: The overlapping letters of the 2019 logo were designed by Baron & Baron, the agency behind many luxury brands.
The high-contrast Didone serif makes a high-street brand look like a fashion magazine.

logoResearch.name: H&M
logoResearch.verifiedFact: H&M started as Hennes, a women's clothing store in Västerås, Sweden, in 1947.
observations: The red, handwritten-style letters make the logo look friendly and fast.
The initials stand for Hennes & Mauritz, after the brand bought the Mauritz Widforss store in 1968.

logoResearch.name: Uniqlo
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Uniqlo opened its first store in Hiroshima, Japan, in 1984, and its current logo was designed by Kashiwa Sato in 2006.
observations: Two red squares hold the name split into two lines, in English and in Japanese katakana.
The square format works as an app icon, a shop sign, and a shopping bag print.

logoResearch.name: Levi's
logoResearch.verifiedFact: Levi Strauss founded the company in San Francisco in 1853, and the batwing logo dates from the late 1960s.
observations: The batwing shape is based on the arched stitching on the back pocket of Levi's jeans.
Bold white letters on red link to the small red tab sewn on every pair of jeans.

listIntro: The boards below show all 45 fashion brand logos in one consistent format, grouped into luxury houses, Paris and Milan labels, designer brands, shoes and accessories, and streetwear and high street.
Each logo is reviewed for its design decisions, not for the brand's size or popularity.
sectionIntroductions: The oldest and most valuable fashion houses rely on heritage: founders' names, monograms, and emblems that have barely changed in decades.
The big Paris and Milan labels show how a typeface can define an era, from Hedi Slimane's minimal sans serifs to the quiet serifs of Bottega Veneta and Loewe.
Designer brands from New York, London, and Germany are mostly named after their founders, and their wordmarks range from preppy serifs to handwriting.
Shoe, bag, and accessory brands have to work on tiny surfaces like soles, clasps, and hardware, so many of them pair a wordmark with a compact symbol.
Streetwear and high-street brands are louder and more graphic, with red boxes, graffiti signatures, and bold colours made for shop fronts and social media.
sectionBridge: This is a visual comparison of fashion brand logos, not a ranking of brands.
Look at how each logo uses type, a monogram, or one detail to signal its price point and personality.
entryFallbacks: The identity relies on a few clear decisions to stay recognizable.
Notice how the logo would look on a label, a shopping bag, and a store front.

findings.heading: Fashion logos are mostly names
findings.text: Almost every brand on this list is named after its founder, from Chanel and Dior to Ralph Lauren and Paul Smith. The wordmark is the logo, so the typeface choice is the whole design.

findings.heading: Monograms turn logos into products
findings.text: Gucci, Louis Vuitton, Fendi, Givenchy, and Tory Burch use initials that also work as prints, clasps, and hardware. A monogram lets customers wear the brand.

findings.heading: Luxury is getting simpler
findings.text: Saint Laurent, Celine, Balenciaga, Burberry, and Ferragamo all simplified their wordmarks in the last decade, dropping first names, accents, or scripts.

findings.heading: Colour is rare, except in streetwear
findings.text: Luxury brands stick to black, while Supreme, H&M, Uniqlo, and Levi's use bold red to stand out on shop fronts and feeds.

logoRosterConfig.checklistHeading: A practical checklist for a fashion brand logo
checklistItems: Does the wordmark work on a woven label, a shopping bag, and a phone screen?
Does the typeface match your price point, from couture serif to streetwear sans?
Could a monogram or symbol work on hardware, prints, and small accessories?
Is it simple enough to embroider, emboss, or print in one colour?
Will it still look right in ten years, or does it follow a short-lived trend?

faq.question: What makes a good fashion brand logo?
faq.answer: A good fashion logo is simple, timeless, and built from carefully chosen type. It works on labels, shopping bags, hardware, and screens, and it signals the brand's price point, like the high-contrast serif of Dior or the bold sans serif of Balenciaga.

faq.question: Why are so many fashion logos just the founder's name?
faq.answer: Most fashion houses started as one designer's studio, like Chanel, Dior, or Ralph Lauren, so the founder's name became the brand. A well-set wordmark carries that personal heritage and is easy to protect as a trademark.

faq.question: What is the difference between a fashion logo and a monogram?
faq.answer: The logo is usually the full brand name, while a monogram combines initials into one mark, like the Gucci GG or the Louis Vuitton LV. Luxury brands use monograms as patterns on bags and fabrics, so the monogram becomes part of the product.

faq.question: What fonts do luxury fashion brands use?
faq.answer: Luxury fashion brands use either high-contrast serif fonts, like Dior, Valentino, and Zara, or clean geometric and grotesque sans serifs, like Chanel, Saint Laurent, and Celine. Most are custom-drawn or heavily adjusted, so they cannot be copied exactly with a free font.

faq.question: What colours do fashion logos use?
faq.answer: Most luxury fashion logos are black so they work on any product and photograph. Colour is more common in streetwear and high street, like the red of Supreme, H&M, Uniqlo, and Levi's.
